note: Plain-language definitions for every abbreviation in a tool's title, labels, help, or sentence (define-build-contracts manifest-extensions: glossary schema). Checked by tools/trust/glossary.test.mjs; relatedTools are filled from the catalog by tools/trust/glossary.mjs --write.

entries.definition: The world's civil time standard, kept within 0.9 s of Earth's rotation by leap seconds. Aviation calls it Zulu time, written with a Z.
A global grid of hexagons (and 12 pentagons) at 16 resolutions, each cell about one-seventh the area of its parent, named by a 15-character index.
A reference atmosphere: 15 °C and 1013.25 hPa at sea level, cooling 6.5 °C per kilometer up to 11 km. Altimeters and performance charts are built on it.
Cartesian X, Y, Z coordinates in meters from Earth's center, turning with the Earth. X points to 0° longitude on the equator and Z to the North Pole.
Height measured from the ground directly below, not from sea level.
The US Department of Defense global reference frame and ellipsoid that GPS uses; the current version is WGS 84.
The WGS ellipsoid and frame defined in 1984 and refined since in realizations such as G2139. GPS positions are in WGS 84.
The manufacturer's handbook for an aircraft: limitations, procedures, performance charts, and weight-and-balance data. Its numbers govern over any calculator.
The FAA-approved manual of an aircraft's limitations and performance. For many light aircraft the POH serves as the AFM.
A distance of exactly 1,852 meters, about one minute of latitude. Aviation and marine navigation measure distance in it.
A grid of 60 zones, each 6° of longitude wide, that turns latitude and longitude into eastings and northings in meters.
The polar companion to UTM, covering the areas north of 84° N and south of 80° S.
Height above the average level of the sea, in practice the geoid. Airport elevations and altimeter altitudes are given above MSL.
An airport weather observation in a standard code: wind, visibility, weather, clouds, temperature, dew point, and altimeter setting, issued at least hourly.
A forecast for an airport, usually 24 or 30 hours long, coded like a METAR with change groups such as FM, TEMPO, BECMG, and PROB30.
The US text forecast of wind direction, wind speed, and temperature at standard altitudes, coded in groups like 2635-08.
A recorded broadcast at busier airports of current weather, runways in use, and notices, updated at least hourly.
The ground width one image pixel covers, such as 2 cm per pixel. A smaller GSD shows more detail.
An Earth ellipsoid defined by the IUGG. GRS 80 underlies NAD 83 and is almost identical to WGS 84.

entries.expansion: International Union of Geodesy and Geophysics
entries.definition: The scientific union that adopted GRS 80 and the mean Earth radius R1.
UTM and UPS coordinates written as a zone, a latitude band, a two-letter 100 km square, and digits, like 17T NE 86309 77770.
MGRS as adopted for US civilian use on NAD 83, usually written with spaces between its parts.
A worldwide grid of 30-minute cells, split into 15- and 5-minute quadrants and keypads, used to name areas.
An aviation grid reference that names 15° and 1° squares with letters, then gives minutes of longitude and latitude.
The NOAA office that defines the US National Spatial Reference System: datums, geoid models, and state plane coordinates.
The part of NOAA that includes the National Geodetic Survey.
The US agency that includes the National Geodetic Survey and the National Weather Service.
Six hours behind UTC, used in the US Mountain time zone during daylight saving time.
The body that publishes the time zone database of names like America/Denver, which this site embeds.
Indicated airspeed corrected for instrument and position error. It measures dynamic pressure, which governs how the aircraft flies.
The airspeed read directly from the airspeed indicator, before any correction.
The aircraft's speed through the air mass. At altitude, where the air is thinner, it is higher than calibrated airspeed.
True airspeed stated in knots.
The EU agency that sets aviation safety rules, including the drone rules in Regulations (EU) 2019/947 and 2019/945.
Height measured from the reference ellipsoid, as GNSS receivers report it. It differs from height above sea level by the geoid height.
The IOGP registry of coordinate reference systems and transformations, each with a code such as EPSG:4326.

entries.expansion: International Earth Rotation and Reference Systems Service
entries.definition: The service that maintains the ITRF and Earth orientation data, and announces leap seconds in Bulletin C.
The global scientific reference frame, realized from thousands of stations whose motions it models. ITRF2020 is current.
The family of North American horizontal datums: NAD 27 on the Clarke 1866 ellipsoid and NAD 83 on GRS 80.
The North American datum on the GRS 80 ellipsoid, fixed to the North American plate. Realizations include NAD 83(2011).
The older North American datum on the Clarke 1866 ellipsoid. Its positions can differ from NAD 83 by tens of meters.
NGS grids that convert positions between US datums, such as NAD 27 to NAD 83, by interpolating measured shifts.
A legacy European datum on the International 1924 ellipsoid.
The legacy datum of the British National Grid, on the Airy 1830 ellipsoid.
A legacy Australian datum on the Australian National Spheroid.
A legacy South American datum on the GRS 1967 ellipsoid.
A global gravity model whose geoid converts GPS ellipsoid heights to heights above mean sea level, to within about a meter.
Local Cartesian coordinates centered on a chosen point, with axes toward east, north, and up.
Local Cartesian axes toward north, east, and down, as aircraft navigation uses them.
Direction and distance from a point: azimuth from north, elevation above the horizontal, and straight-line range.
124 zones of conformal projections on NAD 83, drawn so that distortion stays near 1 part in 10,000 within each zone.
The common web map tile numbering, zoom/x/y, with rows counted from the north edge.
A web map tile numbering like XYZ, but with rows counted from the south edge.
The US satellite navigation system. Its time scale runs a fixed number of seconds ahead of UTC (18 s since 2017) because it never adds leap seconds.
An XML file format for waypoints, routes, and tracks that most GPS devices and mapping apps read.
The FAA's official guide to US flight procedures and air traffic control practice.
The point where an aircraft's weight acts. It must stay inside the envelope in the POH for safe control.
The chord of an equivalent rectangular wing. Larger aircraft state their center-of-gravity limits in percent of it.

entries.expansion: leading edge of the mean aerodynamic chord
entries.definition: The station of the front of the mean aerodynamic chord, from which percent-MAC is measured.
The lowest altitude on a non-precision approach to which a pilot may descend without the runway environment in sight.
A point on a non-precision approach from which a normal descent from the MDA to the runway can begin.
The height of the minimum descent or decision altitude above the touchdown zone elevation.
An EASA drone class: under 900 g, or under 80 J of impact energy, meant for the A1 open subcategory.
The US civil aviation authority.
The codified US federal regulations. Aviation rules are in Title 14, written as 14 CFR.

entries.expansion: American Society for Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
entries.definition: The society that publishes the Positional Accuracy Standards for Digital Geospatial Data used to state map accuracy.
The square root of the average squared difference between measured and true values. ASPRS accuracy classes are stated with it.
The farthest distance at which a remote pilot can still see a drone's position and orientation. EASA ties it to the drone's size.
The distance at which other aircraft can be seen in time to avoid them. EASA takes it as 0.3 times the ground visibility.
Flying where the remote pilot can see the drone without aids. EASA's acceptable distance is the smaller of ALOS and DLOS.
The ITRF2020 plate motion model's code for the North American tectonic plate.
The ITRF2020 plate motion model's code for the Pacific tectonic plate.
The ITRF2020 plate motion model's code for the Eurasian tectonic plate.
The ITRF2020 plate motion model's code for the Australian tectonic plate.
The ITRF2020 plate motion model's code for the South American tectonic plate.
The ITRF2020 plate motion model's code for the Nubian (African) tectonic plate.
An angle written as whole degrees, minutes (1/60 degree), and seconds (1/3600 degree), like 40°26'46".
The time and distance at which two moving aircraft or vessels will pass nearest each other.
On a horizontal curve, where the two straight tangents would meet.
On a horizontal curve, where the curve leaves the back tangent.
On a horizontal curve, where the curve joins the forward tangent.
On a vertical curve, where the two grade lines would meet.
On a vertical curve, where the curve leaves the incoming grade.
On a vertical curve, where the curve joins the outgoing grade.
The US rectangular survey of townships, ranges, and sections, carried out by the federal government since 1785.
A PLSS reference meridian from which ranges are counted east and west.
The continuous atomic time scale. UTC has been TAI minus 37 seconds since 2017.
The Julian date minus 2,400,000.5, so days begin at midnight. MJD 0 is 1858 November 17.
The uniform time scale of astronomical ephemerides: TAI plus 32.184 seconds.
Time kept by Earth's actual rotation. It drifts against atomic time, and UTC is kept within 0.9 s of it.
The difference between Earth-rotation time and UTC, always under 0.9 s, broadcast so users can recover UT1.
The standard text format for GNSS receiver observations. Daily files are named by station, day of year, and year, so any processing service can read them.
The height of the instrument's horizontal axis above the station mark, measured with a tape at setup and added when reducing a sight to an elevation difference.
The height of the prism or target above the point sighted, subtracted when reducing a sight to an elevation difference.
In leveling, the rod reading on a point of known elevation. Added to that elevation it gives the height of the instrument.
In leveling, the rod reading on a point whose elevation is wanted. Subtracted from the height of the instrument it gives that elevation.
The station where the straight tangent ends and a spiral transition begins, curving gradually from straight toward the circular curve.
The station where the entry spiral ends and the circular curve begins, at the curve's full radius.
The station where the circular curve ends and the exit spiral begins.
The station where the exit spiral ends and the alignment is straight again.
A surface built by joining surveyed points into triangles, each flat, so the ground between shots is taken as varying linearly. Volumes and contours are computed from those triangles.
An XML file format for places, paths, and areas on the Earth, read by Google Earth and most mapping apps. Each height says what it is measured from.
A plain-text table with one row per line and the columns separated by commas, which spreadsheets open directly.
A radio aid that shows the straight-line distance from the aircraft to a ground station, in nautical miles. Up high and close in, that slant distance is longer than the distance over the ground.
The rules for flying by reference to instruments under air traffic control, required in clouds and low visibility. IFR flights must carry fuel to an alternate airport and a reserve.
The pressure setting that makes an altimeter read the airport's elevation on the ground, and altitude above sea level in the air.
The air pressure at the airport. With it set, an altimeter reads zero on the ground and height above the airport in the air.
What an altimeter reads with 29.92 inHg (1013.25 hPa) set: the pressure altitude. On the ground it is the field's pressure altitude.
A pressure altitude in hundreds of feet, flown with the altimeter set to 29.92 inHg. FL185 is 18,500 ft of pressure altitude.
The US government weather service, which runs the airport weather stations and computes their altimeter settings.
The radius of a sphere the size of the Earth on average, (2a + b) ÷ 3 = 6,371,008.771 m for WGS 84. Spherical formulas use it when they treat the Earth as a ball.

Measuring a distance by timing light or infrared bounced off a prism or a surface, as a total station does. The air slows the light a little, so the reading is corrected for temperature and pressure, in parts per million.

notAbbreviations.reason: Roman numeral in H3's Class III resolutions
Compass direction, or letters inside example references
Compass direction in PLSS aliquot parts
IUGG symbol for the mean radius, defined in the label
IUGG symbol for the authalic radius, defined in the label
IUGG symbol for the volumetric radius, defined in the label
The product of the meridional and normal radii in √(MN)
Karney's symbol for the geodesic scale, defined in the label
Karney's symbol for the geodesic scale, defined in the label
Karney's symbol for the area under the geodesic, defined in the label
Symbol for the first end area
Symbol for the second end area
Name of a WGS 84 realization (GPS week 2139)
Name of a WGS 84 realization (GPS week 2296)
A station identifier in an example
A flight level written as an example
